meta.title: Algebraic Expressions — Commutative & Associative Properties

overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 7
overview.text: In this lesson, you will master the fundamental properties that allow us to rearrange and group terms in algebraic expressions. You will formalize the commutative properties (order does not matter) and associative properties (grouping does not matter) to construct rigorous proofs of expression equivalence.
outcomes: Use the commutative and associative properties of addition and multiplication to recognize structure within expressions.
Construct step-by-step deductive algebraic proofs demonstrating why two different looking expressions are equivalent.
Explain why subtraction and division are neither commutative nor associative.
overview.teacherInsight: Push students to justify each individual transformation. In algebra, $(pq)r = (qr)p$ is not an obvious identity to a novice; it requires an explicit associative shift followed by a commutative flip.

content.html:
Expression Reordering & Regrouping Playground

Toggle term grouping and order for $(a + b) + c$ vs $a + (b + c)$ and $(ab)c$ vs $(qr)p$.

Value $a$:2
Value $b$:5
Value $c$:8
Addition: $(a + b) + c$ 15 (2 + 5) + 8 = 15
Addition: $a + (b + c)$ 15 2 + (5 + 8) = 15

Multiplicative Associativity & Commutativity:

(ab)c = 80
(ca)b = 80
Proved: $(ab)c = a(bc) = (bc)a = (ca)b$

Formal Mathematical Identities

Commutative Properties

$$a + b = b + a \quad ext{and} \quad ab = ba$$

Order of terms does not affect the resulting sum or product. (True for all real numbers).

Associative Properties

$$(a + b) + c = a + (b + c) \quad ext{and} \quad (ab)c = a(bc)$$

Grouping of consecutive additions or multiplications does not alter the evaluation.

vocabulary.definition: The property stating that the order in which two real numbers are added or multiplied does not change the result: a + b = b + a and ab = ba.
The property stating that the grouping of numbers being added or multiplied does not change the result: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (ab)c = a(bc).
An equality relation A = B such that A and B evaluate to the same value for all possible values of their variables.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sequence of properties rigorously proves the algebraic equivalence of $pqr$ and $qrp$?
options: $pqr = (pq)r = (qp)r = q(pr) = q(rp) = qrp$ using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
$pqr = p(q + r) = pq + pr = qrp$ using the distributive property
$pqr = pqr + 0 = qrp$ using the additive identity property
$pqr = (pqr)^1 = qrp$ using the power of a product rule
practiceQuestions.explanation: From the official Eureka Math Exit Ticket Key: Group $pqr$ as $(pq)r$, apply commutativity to get $(qp)r$, apply associativity to get $q(pr)$, apply commutativity to $pr$ to get $q(rp)$, and rewrite as $qrp$.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is the associative property necessary when reordering three or more multiplied terms like $(a \cdot b) \cdot c$?
options: Because multiplication is formally defined as a binary operation between two elements at a time, so regrouping requires $(ab)c = a(bc)$.
Because numbers cannot be multiplied without converting to fractions first.
Because without associativity, multiplying three numbers always produces zero.
Because variables do not follow standard arithmetic rules unless parenthesized.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Multiplication is strictly a binary operation. The associative property $(ab)c = a(bc)$ allows us to evaluate combinations regardless of parenthetical grouping.

guidedExercises.title: Example 1: Mental Arithmetic Regrouping via Commutative & Associative Laws
guidedExercises.problem: Evaluate $(28 \times 25) \times 4$ using mental arithmetic, explicitly justifying each step. Then simplify the algebraic expression $5(2x - 3) + 4(7 - x)$.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Look for compatible factor pairs that multiply to powers of 10 ($25 \times 4 = 100$). For the polynomial, distribute first, then use commutativity to group like terms.

steps.label: Apply the Associative Property of Multiplication
steps.explanation: Regroup the factors to multiply $25 \times 4$ first.

steps.label: Compute the mental product
steps.explanation: Multiplying by 100 is computed instantly in mental arithmetic.

steps.label: Commute and associate like terms
steps.explanation: Use commutativity to place variable terms together and constants together.

guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Applying commutativity or associativity to subtraction. While $a + b = b + a$, $a - b \neq b - a$. To rearrange terms with subtraction, convert to addition of the opposite: $a - b = a + (-b) = (-b) + a$.

guidedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Proving Non-Equivalence in Subtraction Chains
guidedExercises.problem: Demonstrate that $(a - b) - c \neq a - (b - c)$ by substituting numerical values $a = 12, b = 7, c = 3$. Explain algebraically why associativity fails for subtraction.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Evaluate both parenthetical expressions independently following the order of operations.

steps.label: Evaluate Left-Hand Side $(a - b) - c$
steps.explanation: Perform subtraction inside the parentheses first.

steps.label: Evaluate Right-Hand Side $a - (b - c)$
steps.explanation: Since $2 \neq 8$, the expressions are not equivalent.

steps.label: Algebraic explanation
steps.math: a - (b - c) = a - b + c \neq a - b - c
steps.explanation: Subtracting a difference distributes the negative sign: $-(b - c) = -b + c$.

guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Dropping parentheses when removing a minus sign. Remember $-(b - c) = -b + c$.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 7 Exit Ticket: Algebraic Expressions—The Commutative and Associative Properties
exitTicket.prompt: Write a mathematical proof of the algebraic equivalence of pqr and qrp.
exitTicket.solution:
Proof:
pqr = (pq)r        [By definition of sequential multiplication]
    = (qp)r        [By commutative property of multiplication]
    = q(pr)        [By associative property of multiplication]
    = q(rp)        [By commutative property of multiplication]
    = qrp          [By definition of sequential multiplication]

problems.prompt: Show that the algebraic expression ab + cd is equivalent to dc + ba using commutative properties of addition and multiplication. Justify every step.
problems.solution:
Step 1: ab + cd = ba + cd [Commutative property of multiplication applied to ab]
Step 2: ba + cd = ba + dc [Commutative property of multiplication applied to cd]
Step 3: ba + dc = dc + ba [Commutative property of addition applied to the two terms]
Therefore, ab + cd = dc + ba.

problems.prompt: Is subtraction commutative? Provide a counterexample with specific numbers to prove your claim.
problems.solution: No, subtraction is not commutative. Counterexample: 5 - 3 = 2, but 3 - 5 = -2. Since 2 \ne -2, a - b \ne b - a in general. Subtraction can be rewritten as addition of the opposite: a - b = a + (-b) = (-b) + a.
